messages.subject: Re: packages psych and lavaan
messages.body_plain:
As Ed says, it's not an issue in your case.  It's just saying that both simsem and psych have a function called sim().

But it can become an issue, when you have some code that uses a function, and then you load another library, which has a function with the same name. If you didn't know about this, you might happily load the psych package, and use the sim function. Then you load the simsem package, and use the sim() function again - but now instead of using the psych function, it uses the simsem function, which is kind of different.

The way around this problem is to always reference the package that the function came from. That also makes it easier for other people reading your code to understand what you did (or when you come back to it in the future). You do this by writing:
package::function()

So your code would (if I got it right) look like:

om <- psych::omegaSem(cov(data1), nfactors=3, lavaan=TRUE, n.obs=200, sl=TRUE)
sls.model <- om$omegaSem$model$lavaan
SimSLS1fit200 <- simsem::sim(1000, sls.model, n=200, generate=popModel, lavaanfun = "cfa", std.lv <http://std.lv/>=TRUE)
summary(SimSLS1fit200)

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: Theta parameterisation convergence
messages.body_plain:
Wu  & Estabrook introduce a different order of models compared to Millsap & Yun-Tein. So, in their configural model, you would have:

EXT =~ X2 + X1 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 + X7 # free loadings
EXT ~~ c(1,1)*EXT #fixed factor variance
EXT ~ c(0,0)*EXT #fixed factor mean

X1 | t1 + t2 #free threshold
X1  ~ c(0, 0)*1 #fixed Intercept @0
X1 ~~ c(1,1)*X1 #residual variance @1

just add your other terms and run the model with parameterization = theta. In case of delta, simply replace the residual covariances X1~~ c(1,1)*X1 with the scaling factor: X1 ~*~ X1

You should also get the configural model by just specifying the loadings (better try that), but I felt that specifiying the entire model made it somewhat clearer and easier to introduce the constraints as needed (see terrys response in the other thread).

Best, Felix

messages.body_plain:
Dear group,

I am currently having trouble specifying an alternative identification strategy for longitudinal measurement invariance testing (Widaman, 2010). The part that seems not work is forcing the first item at T1 loading to be estimated freely (I used NA for this) and at the same time constraining the first item loading at T2 to be equal to the first item at T1 (I used equal("") for this).

Here is a minimal working example using the PoliticalDemocracy dataset.

library(lavaan)
mod_wid<-'
  demo60 =~ NA*y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  demo65 =~ equal("demo60=~y1")*y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
  y1 ~~ y5
  y2 ~~ y6
  y3 ~~ y7
  y4 ~~ y8
  demo60 ~ 0*1
  demo60 ~~ 1*demo60
  demo65 ~ NA*1
  demo65 ~~ NA*demo65
  y1 ~ NA*1
  y5 ~ equal("y1 ~ 1")*1
'

fit_wid<-cfa(mod_wid, PoliticalDemocracy, auto.fix.first=F)
summary(fit_wid)

When I run this code (lavaan version 0.5-23.1097) the model will be estimated, however, the estimated loadings for the items y1 and y5 seem to be fixed to 1. I also tried providing an explicit label but to no avail.

Any help is much apprecciated

Gerrit

messages.subject: Re: correlations?
messages.body_plain:
> 1. if I define x as a factor, y as numeric (continuous) in R, depending on the number of the categories of x, lavaan will calculate (point-)biserial/polyserial correlation;
>
> 2. if both x and y are defined as factors, lavaan will calculate tetrachoric/phi/polychoric correlation.
>
> Is that right?

Assuming by factor you mean c("ordered","factor"), it depends whether your model treats both both x and y as random variables.
For exogenous observed variables, lavaan calculates Phi (just a Pearson correlation between dummy codes) or point-*serial (Pearson correlation between dummy codes and other exogenous continuous predictors) from sample statistics and just treats them as fixed (if fixed.x = TRUE), or estimates them (if fixed.x = FALSE).
For endogenous variables, lavaan instead estimates *choric or *serial correlations, which make the assumption of a normally distributed latent item response behind each observed ordered factor.

So if you are literally just running a "model" to estimate a bivariate correlation between 2 variables (with no other modeled effects), then I think you would have to treat them as single-indicators of factors (and therefore endogenous), whose (model-implied) correlation will be estimated.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> I actually would like to constraint residual variances to be > 0. Is there any not-so-complicated way to do it?

The EFA model syntax is automatically generated, but you can indirectly add additional constraints as model-syntax commands passed to lavaan() via the constraints argument.  If you use parTable(fit) to extract the parameter table from the unrotated lavaan object, you can see which labels lavaan generates for the residual variances.

unrotated <- efaUnrotate(HolzingerSwineford1939, nf = 3, varList = paste0("x", 1:9))
PT <- parTable(unrotated)
PT[PT$op == "~~", ]

> 42 42 factor2 ~~ factor3     1    1    0      0   0           1  .p42. 0.000 0.000 0.000
> 43 43      x1 ~~      x1     1    0   37     NA   0           1  .p43. 0.679 0.696 0.087
> 44 44      x2 ~~      x2     1    0   38     NA   0           1  .p44. 0.691 1.035 0.102
> 45 45      x3 ~~      x3     1    0   39     NA   0           1  .p45. 0.637 0.692 0.097

You see that the residual variances for x1-x9 are labeled ".p43." - ".p51.", so you can add inequality constraints when you run the model again.

unrotated <- efaUnrotate(HolzingerSwineford1939, nf = 3, varList = paste0("x", 1:9),
                         constraints = positiveVariances)

However, I would not recommend constrained estimation as a solution for Heywood cases.  Constraining it potentially masks other problems with your model, and forcing negative estimates to be positive will bias other model parameters.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150

Instead, test whether the Heywood case is consistent with sampling error:

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Kenneth_Bollen/publication/228937678_Testing_Negative_Error_Variances_Is_a_Heywood_Case_a_Symptom_of_Misspecification/links/00b495274eb519224c000000.pdf

If sampling error cannot be discounted (because the 95% CI includes positive values), and your model fits well, then it is reasonable to assume the Heywood case is due to sampling error rather than model misspecification.  But EFA models are exploratory models anyway, not particularly well suited to represent specific theoretical models.

> So, why is that? Is this to be expected since ML is not appropriate for ordinal data? Or are the models more different than i think?

I would try asking about this on SEMNET, since it is not about using lavaan (you would have the same question if your results were from Mplus).

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

But I think you are right, the models are more different than you think.  With DWLS, you constrained all intercepts to be zero, and thresholds were estimated relative to that assumed location of the latent item-response distribution.  With ML, you estimated intercepts, so they were nonzero (and equal across groups).  So the location (and scale) of the latent item-response distributions are different under DWLS than the distributions of the observed "continuous" indicators under ML, and that has (perhaps complicated) implications for the estimated common factor that has an assumed linear effect on those latent item-response distributions.

As a point of curiosity, you could simply try fixing the intercepts in the DWLS model to the estimated values from the ML model.  The model would be statistically equivalent, but thresholds would be estimated relative to those locations, which would in turn affect the latent means.  Might help you think about the problem, but no guarantee that the result would agree with your intuition any more than the current result does.

la.model <- '

fit <- lavaan(la.model, data=j2$data$observed, estimator='DWLS',

               auto.th <http://auto.th>=TRUE,
               auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE, parameterization="delta")

reasonable defaults:

fit <- sem(la.model, data=j2$data$observed, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

messages.subject: Re: Correlating residuals of indicators
messages.body_plain:
A common factor is not a composite. If it were, then your strategy would make sense, but it is not. You cannot allow all free residual covariances and estimate a factor model. The factor is constructed out of the covariances among the observed variables--the factor "explains" and "accounts for" these covariances, because all the observed variables are jointly dependent on the factor. If all residual covariances are free, there is nothing for the common factor to explain, and statistical identification will fail. The principle of "conditional independence" states that, if the common factor model is strictly correct, then the residuals for the observed variables will be uncorrelated, because all of their shared variance has been accounted for by the factor. Any good text on factor analysis should make these points.

messages.subject: Re: Questions on cross-lagged panel model
messages.body_plain:
> Q1: do we proceed with two-step procedure? First is CFA. Second is SEM. I don't think so because the 2 should give us the same results.

If your latent structure is saturated, then df between CFA and SEM will be equivalent, and the models will be statistically equivalent.  But CFA could still be useful for testing invariance of measurement parameters across occasions before drawing inferences about effects over time.

> Q2: With cross-lagged, we can go for either correlated residual or uncorrelated residual. Conceptually, are there any differences?

Yes, correlated residuals between the same item over time represent the theory that the same item-specific (but not common-factor) component of the indicator affects it over time, and those effects over time are correlated for the same reason you allow common factors to correlated with themselves over time.

> Q3: I downloaded some lavaan examples from Dr. Newsom's website (http://www.longitudinalsem.com/).. Why should we repeat the variable "w1happy "  and use "NA" at first？ The first loading is already set to 1 by default

>
>      w1posaff =~ NA*w1happy + (lambda1)*w1happy

That is only necessary to do 2 things to the same parameter: freely estimate it (NA*w1happy) and give that estimate a label (lambda1*w1happy), which makes it easier to apply equality constraints by specifying the same label for multiple parameters.

The freeing part would not be necessary if you identified the model by standardizing the latent variable (std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE) instead of fixing a loading to 1. messages.body_plain:
I was also struggling following this example (but I acknowledge that this topic is neither simple nor straight-forward, regardless of the toy example).  In the spirit of Keith's recommendation, I am posting here a smaller example, and in fact reproducible because I set a seed before generating data.  I also generated data from a factor model so that it would be more likely to converge on a solution than the example generating independent vectors (no common factor).

I apply different thresholds to the same latent item-responses to generate binary and 3-category data, and a mixture (2 of each type).  I only fit models to the ternary data to get the ball rolling.  I noticed that in Felix's and in Giacomo's syntax for fitting Millsap & Yun-Tein's model, the residual variances were mistakenly fixed to 1 in all groups ("# ALL UNIQUE VARIANCES TO 1") rather than only the first group.  For binary data, only the marker-variable's residual variance would also have to be fixed to 1 in other groups.  Here's a summary of the rules in Appendix A of M's article:

http://sunthud.com/catInvariance.html

Anyway, when I free those residual variances in the example below, and when I free the factor variances in group 1 (which the previous examples also failed to do for the MYT parameterization), the models all have the same df.

As Felix & Giacomo point out, the df returned by lav_partable_df() is not consistent with the correct df reported by fitMeasures() when the model includes constraints, presumably because lav_partable_npar() returns the count of all free parameters without subtracting out the number of equality constraints at the bottom of the parameter table.

N <- 1000
pop <- ' F1 =~ .6*X1 + .7*X2 + .8*X3 + .9*X4 '
## generate normal latent-response data
dat <- simulateData(pop, model.type = "cfa", sample.nobs = N,
                    standardized = TRUE, std.lv = TRUE, seed = 12345,
                    empirical = TRUE)
## apply thresholds for binary data
dat2 <- data.frame(lapply(dat, cut, breaks = c(-Inf, 0, Inf),
                          ordered_result = TRUE))
dat2$group <- 1:2
## apply thresholds for ternary data
dat3 <- data.frame(lapply(dat, cut, breaks = c(-Inf, -.5, .5, Inf),
                          ordered_result = TRUE))
dat3$group <- 1:2
## mixture of binary and ternary data
mix <- cbind(dat3[c("X1","X2")], dat2[c("X3","X4")])

#### fit models to 3-category data

# CONFIGURAL as in Wu Estabrook Condition 7

mod.c7.3 <- "
F1 =~ c(NA, NA)*X1 + X2 + X3 + X4

X1 | t1 + t2
X2 | t1 + t2
X3 | t1 + t2
X4 | t1 + t2

X1  ~ c(0, 0)*1
X2  ~ c(0, 0)*1
X3  ~ c(0, 0)*1
X4  ~ c(0, 0)*1

X1 ~*~ c(1, 1)*X1
X2 ~*~ c(1, 1)*X2
X3 ~*~ c(1, 1)*X3
X4 ~*~ c(1, 1)*X4

F1  ~~ c(1, 1)*F1
F1   ~ c(0, 0)*1
"

# CONFIGURAL as in Wu Estabrook Condition 8
mod.c8.3 <- "
F1 =~ c(NA, NA)*X1 + X2 + X3 + X4

X1 | t1 + t2
X2 | t1 + t2
X3 | t1 + t2
X4 | t1 + t2

X1  ~ c(0, 0)*1
X2  ~ c(0, 0)*1
X3  ~ c(0, 0)*1
X4  ~ c(0, 0)*1

X1 ~~ c(1, 1)*X1
X2 ~~ c(1, 1)*X2
X3 ~~ c(1, 1)*X3
X4 ~~ c(1, 1)*X4

F1 ~~ c(1, 1)*F1
F1  ~ c(0, 0)*1
"

# Millsap & Yun-Tein's (MYT) parameterization
mod.myt3 <- "
F1 =~ c(1, 1)*X1 + X2 + X3 + X4
X1 | c(t1_1, t1_1)*t1 + c(t2_1, t2_1)*t2
X2 | c(t1_2, t1_2)*t1 + t2

X3 | c(t1_3, t1_3)*t1 + t2
X4 | c(t1_4, t1_4)*t1 + t2

X1  ~ c(0, 0)*1
X2  ~ c(0, 0)*1
X3  ~ c(0, 0)*1
X4  ~ c(0, 0)*1

X1 ~~ c(1, NA)*X1
X2 ~~ c(1, NA)*X2
X3 ~~ c(1, NA)*X3
X4 ~~ c(1, NA)*X4

F1 ~~ c(NA, NA)*F1
F1  ~ c( 0, NA)*1
"

fit.c7.3 <- cfa(mod.c7.3, data = dat3, group = "group", parameterization="delta")
fit.c8.3 <- cfa(mod.c8.3, data = dat3, group = "group", parameterization="theta")
fit.myt3 <- cfa(mod.myt3, data = dat3, group = "group", parameterization="theta")

WED <- partable(fit.c7.3)
WET <- partable(fit.c8.3)
MYT <- partable(fit.myt3) # does not subtract constraints

lav_partable_npar(WED)
lav_partable_npar(WET)
lav_partable_npar(MYT)

lav_partable_ndat(WED)
lav_partable_ndat(WET)
lav_partable_ndat(MYT)

lav_partable_df(WED)
lav_partable_df(WET)
lav_partable_df(MYT) # wrong
fitmeasures(fit.myt3, "df") # correct

WED #[WED$op %in% c("~~","~*~"), ]
WET #[WET$op %in% c("~~","~*~"), ]
MYT #[MYT$op %in% c("~~","~*~"), ]

Hey Keith,

thanks for your kind help and time.

@Terrence: your post came exactly as I was writing the below, so pardon the duplication. The issue was precisely that of the unique variances!

What I'm trying to do is indeed to compare equivalent parameterisations of the same model, following Wu and Estabrook (2016), WE henceforth.

Using the data and example code at Sunthud's webpage <http://sunthud.com/catInvariance.html>, I've finally figured out how to implement these parameterisations in lavaan:
the MYT parameterisation (from Millsap and Yun-Tein, 2004)
the WE delta parameterisation (condition 7 in WE)
the WE theta parameterisation (condition 8 in WE)
an alternative parameterisation similar to WE theta, which relaxes equality of latent means and variances by restricting the loading and one threshold on an item for each factor.

messages.body_plain:
> It still puzzles me why the lav_partable_df() function returns different
> values than fitmeasures(, "df"), as you can see in the example... But
> maybe it's intended behaviour

It is intended indeed.

lav_partable_df() does not take into account the number of
(non-redundant) equality constraints. For the latter, I need to compute
the rank of the 'constraints matrix', which is not stored in the
parameter table (the input of lav_partable_df), but in the
@Mo...@con.jac slot.

This is the relevant code snippet in lavaan (in lav_test.R):

# degrees of freedom
     df <- lav_partable_df(lavpartable)

     # handle equality constraints (note: we ignore inequality constraints,
     # active or not!)
     # we use the rank of con.jac (even if the constraints are nonlinear)
     if(nrow(lavm...@con.jac) > 0L) {
         ceq.idx <- attr(lavm...@con.jac, "ceq.idx")
         if(length(ceq.idx) > 0L) {
             neq <- qr(lavm...@con.jac[ceq.idx,,drop=FALSE])$rank
             df <- df + neq
         }
     }

The code of lav_partable_df() is simply:

lav_partable_df(partable)
{
     npar <- lav_partable_npar(partable)
     ndat <- lav_partable_ndat(partable)
     df <- ndat - npar
     as.integer(df)
}

To get the 'correct' df, there two ways. Either using fitMeasures(), or
by using:

lavInspect(fit, "test")[[1]]$df

Yves.
